newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: ICE HOCKEY-RIFT COULD DERAIL CZECH HOPES OF WORLD TITLE.
newsitem.headline: ICE HOCKEY-RIFT COULD DERAIL CZECH HOPES OF WORLD TITLE.

text.p: A rift between some of the Czech Republic's best players and coach Ludek Bukac is threatening to derail the country's attempt to retain the world title in Finland starting this April.

National Hockey League goal scoring leader Jaromir Jagr, and top Czech Extraliga goaltender Roman Cechmanek have said they will never again play for Bukac, branding him arrogant, incompetent and dishonest. Others appear set to follow.
"In America, coaches respect their players' opinions," said Jagr. "Czech coaches are like communists. They must have the upper hand at all costs."

Since becoming coach of the national team in 1994, Bukac has driven out many top players, but also guided the Czechs last year to their first world championship since the former Czechoslovakia won the last of its six titles in 1985.

And he puts the blame for the team's dismal performance since winning the title in Vienna squarely on the shoulders of the players themselves. The Czechs have won only three of 18 games including an embarrassing 7-1 loss to Germany as they crashed out of the World Cup.
"The players couldn't have expected us to applaud their performances. The losses were their fault," he said.

Bukac said there were too many NHL players on the World Cup team and that he preferred Extraliga players to form the nucleus of the national team. "This strategy worked for us at last year's world championships," he said.
However, this may prove a difficult strategy to follow since two key Extraliga players have already ruled out taking part at the upcoming world championships.
Veteran defenceman Drahomir Kadlec said he was humiliated by the national team's pitiful performance at last month's Sweden Cup where they finished last, losing three out of four games.

The 31-year-old defenceman, who was a second team all-star at last year's world championships, complained Bukac gave the players almost no instruction on the ice in Sweden, and then shirked responsibility for the team's poor performance.
"No one told us what to do during the games," he said, "and when we lost, the coaches didn't accept any responsibility. They looked for excuses."
At the end of the Swedish tournament, Bukac told reporters that his players had not been prepared mentally or physically, and he criticised their performance at both ends of the ice.
"We made far too many mistakes. You can't do that in international hockey because it is much faster and opponents capitalise on mistakes," he said.
Kadlec said relationships on the team, particularly between the coaching staff and players, need to be improved.

Cechmanek has also dismissed the possibility of playing on the national team under Bukac, which could be the costliest blow to the defending champions given their recent penchant for conceding soft goals.

Last month, Cechmanek, who has led Vsetin to two consecutive Extraliga titles, denounced Bukac as "a liar" who had promised the goalie the number one spot on the national team only to look for someone else to fill that position when veteran netminder Roman Turek left for the NHL.
"There is no chance of me playing on the team," said an indignant Cechmanek.
Bukac's response was pointed. "I never make promises about the roster, and a player who doesn't accept this doesn't stand a chance of making the team."
And not many people stand a chance of getting along with Bukac, according to Michal Stepanovsky, a hockey writer at the Czech newspaper Pravo.
"Bukac doesn't tolerate anyone having a different opinion from him," Stepanovsky said. "No one can work with him anymore. The only one who can is (assistant coach) Zdenek Uher."
Nonetheless, Czech Ice Hockey Association Chairman Karel Gut is standing behind Bukac.
"We aren't going to fire him. We don't think that the problems with the team are entirely his fault. Besides, we will never bow to pressure from players," Gut said.
